title: Gambhir 'Concerned' by India's Batting Collapses After 244-Run Rout in New Zealand
excerpt: India folded for 89 chasing 334 at Mount Maunganui, their second-heaviest ODI defeat. The head coach said the repeat collapses — not one bad innings — are the problem, in conditions he called the closest thing to next year's World Cup.
body:
• India were bowled out for 89 in 26.4 overs chasing 334 at Mount Maunganui, a 244-run defeat that Reuters reported as their second-heaviest in ODI history.
  • Matt Henry took 6 for 27, removing Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer for ducks in the first over of the chase; Will Young made 125 for New Zealand.
  • Head coach Gautam Gambhir said the collapses concern him because New Zealand conditions are the closest India will get to next year's World Cup in Southern Africa.
  • India still lead the five-match series 2-1, with the final ODI at the same venue on Sunday.

India's head coach did not hide behind the series scoreline. Hours after his side were bowled out for 89 in a 244-run defeat by New Zealand in the fourth ODI at Mount Maunganui — a loss Reuters and ANI reported as India's second-biggest by runs in one-day internationals — Gautam Gambhir said the pattern of batting collapses, not just this one innings, is what worries him with the World Cup less than a year away.

Chasing 334 on Friday, India lost Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and captain Shreyas Iyer for ducks in Matt Henry's first over and never recovered, folding in 26.4 overs. Henry, playing his first match of the series, finished with 6 for 27. New Zealand's 333 was built on Will Young's 125 off 108 balls, with support from Tim Seifert (58) and Finn Allen (41). Only Ishan Kishan (27), Axar Patel (21) and Naman Dhir (21) reached double figures for India.

"I will be concerned because obviously these are conditions which are going to be closest to what we might get during the World Cup."

— Gautam Gambhir, India head coach

Not one bad day

Gambhir's point was that Friday was a repeat. "There's no benefit to sweeping it under the carpet," he said, according to ESPNcricinfo. "It isn't just this match. Even in the previous match, we were seven down for 111 or 112. Today we lost, so we are talking about it." In that second ODI, India had slipped to 111 for 7 chasing 135 in a rain-affected game they narrowly won by the DLS method. "If you're chasing 135, and you get seven down for 111, obviously it is a bit of a concern, because yes, there is some help here for the bowlers, so we have to be not only mentally but from the skill point of view ready as well."

He rejected the idea that the bowling was unplayable. The problem, he said, was the length Henry hit — too full to go back to, too short to get forward to — and batters getting stuck on the crease: "More than the wobble seam, it is where we got stuck in the crease was the problem." He also set the terms for batting in these conditions: "You aren't going to score 70-80 in the first 10 overs. If you're 35-40 for no loss, that is also good enough. In India, the easiest time for batting is the first 10-15 overs. Here it's probably the hardest time."

Why the World Cup makes it urgent

The 2027 ODI World Cup will be hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, where pitches are expected to offer a genuine contest between bat and ball rather than the batter-friendly surfaces of the subcontinent, Reuters noted. That is precisely Gambhir's fear: "When you play in India, obviously you all know that there is hardly anything for the bowlers, but when you come in these conditions, you know that there is actually a good contest between bat and ball, so this is probably the closest [conditions to the World Cup]." The bigger concern from Friday, he added, was not the margin but the speed — "how quickly we got bundled out," in around 26 or 27 overs.

India did not help themselves in the field: Auqib Nabi found Young's edge twice early only for Rohit and Ishan Kishan to put down back-to-back chances, and Young made them pay with his hundred. "Had we got Will Young in that first couple of overs, probably things could have been a lot different," Gambhir conceded. "No one else did [drop him]. We did, so we had to pay for it."

What happens next

India still lead the five-match series 2-1 — the third ODI was abandoned because of rain — and New Zealand cannot win the series, but they can level it in Sunday's final match at the same venue. For Gambhir, that game is now an examination: whether a batting line-up with this much experience can adapt to conditions he expects to meet again, with far more at stake, in Southern Africa next year.
